summary: Russia issues a unified 16-day e-visa to citizens of some 60 countries including most of the EU, admits CIS neighbours and much of Latin America and the Gulf visa-free, and requires an embassy visa from US, UK, Canadian and Australian travellers. Note that most Western governments currently advise against all travel to Russia.

notes: Drones and satellite communication equipment are heavily restricted — bringing them in can lead to confiscation or prosecution.
Medicines containing controlled substances need a prescription and may require a customs declaration on arrival.

payments.text: Visa and Mastercard issued outside Russia do not work anywhere in the country — bring US dollars or euros in cash to exchange, and budget for the whole trip. Russian-issued Mir cards are accepted almost everywhere domestically.

safety.text: Most Western governments currently advise against all travel to Russia because of the war in Ukraine, drone attacks, limited flights and consular help, and the risk of arbitrary detention — with dual nationals facing exit bans and mobilisation rules. Everyday street crime is low away from border regions, but the overall situation warrants treating travel as high-risk.

bestTimeToVisit.text: May to September brings warm weather and long daylight for Moscow, St Petersburg's White Nights and the Golden Ring towns; winter is atmospheric but very cold.

tips.text: The US, UK, EU and most Western governments advise against all travel to Russia — flights are limited, consular help is minimal, and dual nationals face additional risks including exit bans. Check your own government's advice before booking.
Foreign Visa and Mastercard cards do not work in Russia — carry enough cash in US dollars or euros to exchange on arrival, and keep exchange receipts.

The unified e-visa is single-entry, valid 60 days for a stay of up to 16 days, and only usable at approved border crossings listed on evisa.kdmid.ru — check that your planned entry point is on the list.

Stays of more than 7 working days must be registered with the migration authorities — hotels do this automatically, but private hosts must arrange it, and missing registration can cause fines on exit.
Stay well away from regions bordering Ukraine and from the North Caucasus republics — drone activity, security incidents and access restrictions make them genuinely dangerous.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Russia?
faq.answer: Most travellers do. Citizens of around 60 countries — including most EU states, China's SARs excepted, India, Japan and several Gulf monarchies — can use the unified 16-day e-visa, while CIS neighbours, much of Latin America and a handful of bilateral partners enter visa-free. US, UK, Canadian, Australian and New Zealand citizens must obtain a visa from a Russian consulate.

faq.question: Can US or UK citizens get the Russian e-visa?
faq.answer: No. The United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and New Zealand are not on the e-visa eligibility list, so their citizens need a full consular visa with an invitation or booking confirmation — and limited bilateral relations can make appointments and processing slow.

faq.question: How does the Russian unified e-visa work?
faq.answer: You apply online at evisa.kdmid.ru, pay about USD 52, and the visa is normally issued within four calendar days. It is single-entry, valid for 60 days from issue, allows a stay of up to 16 days, and can only be used at approved border crossings.

faq.question: Is it safe to travel to Russia right now?
faq.answer: Most Western governments advise against all travel to Russia. Everyday crime affecting tourists is low in the big cities, but the war in Ukraine, occasional drone strikes, limited flights and consular support, and the risk of arbitrary detention mean travel carries real risks — dual Russian nationals face extra rules including possible exit restrictions.

faq.question: Can I pay by card in Russia?
faq.answer: Not with a foreign card — Visa and Mastercard issued outside Russia stopped working there in 2022. Bring cash in US dollars or euros to exchange for rubles, or arrange a domestic Mir card for a longer stay.

faq.question: Do I need to register my stay in Russia?
faq.answer: Yes, if you stay more than 7 working days. Hotels register guests automatically; if you stay privately, your host must register you with the migration authorities. Keep your migration card and registration slip — they can be checked on departure.
